cards.explanation: Identify the level of organisation rather than calling every small circular profile a whole lobe.
cards.text: The terminal duct and associated lobules form a {{c1::terminal ductal lobular unit}}.
cards.question: The terminal duct and associated lobules form a {{c1::terminal ductal lobular unit}}.

cards.explanation: Many acini form a lobule; many lobules occur within a lobe.
cards.text: The small secretory unit within a breast lobule is an {{c1::acinus}}.
cards.question: The small secretory unit within a breast lobule is an {{c1::acinus}}.

cards.explanation: The myoepithelial layer lies outside it, within the basement-membrane boundary.
cards.text: The epithelial cell layer facing an acinar lumen is the {{c1::luminal layer}}.
cards.question: The epithelial cell layer facing an acinar lumen is the {{c1::luminal layer}}.

cards.explanation: Recognising these layers is important when assessing whether a lesion is in situ.
cards.text: Myoepithelial cells lie between luminal cells and the {{c1::basement membrane}}.
cards.question: Myoepithelial cells lie between luminal cells and the {{c1::basement membrane}}.

cards.explanation: A diagnosis depends on organisation as well as individual-cell appearance.
cards.text: Histology evaluates cellular relationships and tissue {{c1::architecture}}.
cards.question: Histology evaluates cellular relationships and tissue {{c1::architecture}}.

cards.explanation: Immunohistochemistry is required to evaluate these protein markers.
cards.text: H&E alone cannot determine ER, PR or {{c1::HER2 status}}.
cards.question: H&E alone cannot determine ER, PR or {{c1::HER2 status}}.

cards.explanation: A two-dimensional section must be interpreted within three-dimensional tissue anatomy.
cards.text: Different cutting angles can make the same duct appear to have different {{c1::shapes}}.
cards.question: Different cutting angles can make the same duct appear to have different {{c1::shapes}}.

cards.explanation: Lipid is removed during routine processing, leaving characteristic clear profiles.
cards.text: Large clear spaces corresponding to fat cells identify {{c1::adipose tissue}} in routine breast sections.
cards.question: Large clear spaces corresponding to fat cells identify {{c1::adipose tissue}} in routine breast sections.

cards.explanation: Historical estimates in the slide do not predict the outcome of an individual untreated lesion.
cards.text: DCIS is a precursor lesion but progression to invasion is {{c1::not inevitable}}.
cards.question: DCIS is a precursor lesion but progression to invasion is {{c1::not inevitable}}.

cards.explanation: Shared environment and multiple inherited factors can also contribute.
cards.text: Familial clustering of breast cancer does not always establish a single {{c1::hereditary pathogenic variant}}.
cards.question: Familial clustering of breast cancer does not always establish a single {{c1::hereditary pathogenic variant}}.

cards.explanation: This is one explanation for their association with breast-cancer risk; it is not a deterministic outcome.
cards.text: Earlier menarche and later menopause increase the duration of {{c1::ovarian hormone exposure}}.
cards.question: Earlier menarche and later menopause increase the duration of {{c1::ovarian hormone exposure}}.

cards.explanation: Distinguish it from menopause, the permanent cessation of cycles.
cards.text: The onset of menstrual periods is {{c1::menarche}}.
cards.question: The onset of menstrual periods is {{c1::menarche}}.

cards.explanation: Most cases are not explained by a single recognised inherited syndrome.
cards.text: Absence of an obvious family history does not exclude {{c1::breast cancer}}.
cards.question: Absence of an obvious family history does not exclude {{c1::breast cancer}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture also illustrates ultrasound and MRI for different clinical roles.
cards.text: The breast-screening modality based on X-rays is {{c1::mammography}}.
cards.question: The breast-screening modality based on X-rays is {{c1::mammography}}.

cards.explanation: The slide's statement that benign lesions cannot grow is incorrect; the key distinction is malignant behaviour.
cards.text: A benign breast lump can {{c1::grow}} without invading or metastasising.
cards.question: A benign breast lump can {{c1::grow}} without invading or metastasising.

cards.explanation: A palpable lump is not automatically a malignant tumour.
cards.text: A fluid-filled breast lesion is a {{c1::cyst}}.
cards.question: A fluid-filled breast lesion is a {{c1::cyst}}.

cards.explanation: Distinguish a benign solid tumour from a fluid-filled cyst.
cards.text: The benign breast tumour example named in the lecture is a {{c1::fibroadenoma}}.
cards.question: The benign breast tumour example named in the lecture is a {{c1::fibroadenoma}}.

cards.explanation: The slide explicitly cautions that the term does not imply benign behaviour in every case.
cards.text: Phyllodes tumours can be benign, borderline or {{c1::malignant}}.
cards.question: Phyllodes tumours can be benign, borderline or {{c1::malignant}}.

cards.explanation: Their expression can guide endocrine treatment rather than defining invasion by itself.
cards.text: ER and PR are {{c1::hormone receptors}}.
cards.question: ER and PR are {{c1::hormone receptors}}.

cards.explanation: The slide's BRCA expansion is misleading; inherited pathogenic variants can confer susceptibility.
cards.text: BRCA1/BRCA2 are gene names, not a {{c1::breast carcinoma antigen}} test.
cards.question: BRCA1/BRCA2 are gene names, not a {{c1::breast carcinoma antigen}} test.

cards.explanation: It does not by itself decide whether a lobular lesion is invasive.
cards.text: Loss of E-cadherin supports {{c1::lobular differentiation}}.
cards.question: Loss of E-cadherin supports {{c1::lobular differentiation}}.

cards.explanation: A preserved surrounding layer supports an in situ interpretation in the appropriate architecture.
cards.text: p63, SMA and calponin help identify the {{c1::myoepithelial layer}}.
cards.question: p63, SMA and calponin help identify the {{c1::myoepithelial layer}}.

cards.explanation: Treatment and prognosis require more context than the slide's broad description of this group.
cards.text: Negative ER, PR and HER2 results define a {{c1::triple-negative receptor profile}}.
cards.question: Negative ER, PR and HER2 results define a {{c1::triple-negative receptor profile}}.

cards.explanation: The source contrasts this with a solid cellular fill.
cards.text: Punched-out luminal spaces within a DCIS cell sheet form a {{c1::cribriform pattern}}.
cards.question: Punched-out luminal spaces within a DCIS cell sheet form a {{c1::cribriform pattern}}.

cards.explanation: Calcification may accompany necrosis; it does not itself establish invasion.
cards.text: Central necrotic material in a DCIS duct suggests the {{c1::comedo pattern}}.
cards.question: Central necrotic material in a DCIS duct suggests the {{c1::comedo pattern}}.

cards.explanation: Assess the boundary and surrounding stroma rather than relying on cellular crowding alone.
cards.text: An expanded duct containing atypical cells but no basement-membrane breach is consistent with {{c1::DCIS}}.
cards.question: An expanded duct containing atypical cells but no basement-membrane breach is consistent with {{c1::DCIS}}.

cards.explanation: In situ versus invasive depends on the boundary, not E-cadherin alone.
cards.text: Dyscohesive cells filling acini without stromal invasion support {{c1::LCIS}}.
cards.question: Dyscohesive cells filling acini without stromal invasion support {{c1::LCIS}}.

cards.explanation: This is a tissue-pattern comparison rather than a definitive diagnosis from one tiny image.
cards.text: Irregular cohesive nests within desmoplastic stroma favour {{c1::invasive ductal carcinoma}}.
cards.question: Irregular cohesive nests within desmoplastic stroma favour {{c1::invasive ductal carcinoma}}.

cards.explanation: The source also illustrates targetoid growth around ducts and lobules.
cards.text: Single-file dyscohesive cells infiltrating stroma favour {{c1::invasive lobular carcinoma}}.
cards.question: Single-file dyscohesive cells infiltrating stroma favour {{c1::invasive lobular carcinoma}}.

cards.explanation: This differs from an in situ lesion contained within breast ducts.
cards.text: Breast carcinoma growing in an axillary lymph node represents {{c1::metastasis}}.
cards.question: Breast carcinoma growing in an axillary lymph node represents {{c1::metastasis}}.

cards.explanation: The practice micrographs have no reliable answer key in the slides. No exact slide-by-slide diagnosis has been invented.
cards.text: Before naming an unkeyed breast micrograph, determine whether atypical cells are confined or {{c1::invading stroma}}.
cards.question: Before naming an unkeyed breast micrograph, determine whether atypical cells are confined or {{c1::invading stroma}}.

Each breast has around 10-15 lobes
Each lobes contain smaller lobules

The space between the lobules and the ducts is filled with fat

slides.text:
Breast Cancer
Breast cancer is the most common cancer in the UK, despite the fact that it is rare in men. 

Breast cancer is by far the commonest cancer in women in the UK accounting for 31% of all cases in women and accounts for around 16% of female death (Cancer Research UK)









With the advent of the screening programme approximately 20% of  detected breast cancers are Ductal Carcinoma In Situ (DCIS). 

Evidence suggests that DCIS is the precursor to invasive breast cancer in most cases.  (JL Jones, 2006, Br Ca Res)


Other studies have suggested that left untreated as many as 50% of DCIS cases will not progress in the life-time of the patient (L. Collins et al. 2005, Cancer; M Saunders et al, 2005, Cancer).

4th most common cause of cancer death in the UK

Risk Factors
Unchangeable risk factors: Gender, Age, Genetics, family history, race, dense breast tissues, younger age at onset of menstrual periods/later age at on set of menopause
Changeable risk factors:
No breast feeding, no children or later age at first live birth, hormone replacement treatment, birth control pills, geography, alcohol, post-menopausal obesity, lack of exercise.

slides.text:
Benign – A lump of cells that can NOT grow or spread.
Malignant – Tumour cells that can grow and spread. 
Fibroadenomas-benign
Breast Cysts-fluid filled sacs in the breast they can feel soft or hard and can be painful. Many cysts go away by themselves, if they are large and sore they can be drained using a needle. 
Benign phyllodes tumor-A phyllodes tumour can be benign (non-cancerous) or malignant (cancerous). They are rare and in older women. These tumours are usually removed by a small operation (surgery). 
A breast lump does not always mean cancer!

slides.text:
Immunohistochemistry (IHC) Markers

E-cadherin: present in IDC, lost in ILC/LCIS
ER/PR: hormone receptor status
HER2: target for trastuzumab
Ki-67: proliferation index
Myoepithelial markers (p63, SMA, calponin): confirm in situ lesions

slides.topic: Breast Cancer Practical Lecture — Anatomy, Screening & Recognition — source 21
slides.text:
Molecular Subtypes

Luminal A: ER+, PR+, HER2–, low Ki-67 → hormonal therapy
Luminal B: ER+, PR±, HER2±, high Ki-67 → more aggressive
HER2-enriched: ER–, PR–, HER2+ → targeted therapy
Triple-negative: ER–, PR–, HER2– → chemo-sensitive, poor prognosis

slides.text:
Ductal Carcinoma In Situ (DCIS)

Non-invasive; confined within ducts, no basement membrane invasion
Architectural patterns: comedo, cribriform, papillary, micropapillary, solid
Comedo: central necrosis, high grade, calcifications
Myoepithelial layer preserved; seen on H&E and confirmed by IHC
Detected via mammographic microcalcifications

slides.text:
Lobular Carcinoma In Situ (LCIS)
Non-invasive; confined to lobules/acini, no basement membrane invasion
Usually incidental finding, often not associated with calcifications
Architectural pattern: filling and distension of acini by small, uniform, dyshesive cells
Cells: round nuclei, scant cytoplasm; loss of E-cadherin expression (IHC confirmation)
Myoepithelial layer preserved
Often multifocal and bilateral

Invasive Ductal Carcinoma (IDC)

Most common invasive type (~70–80%)
Irregular nests or cords in desmoplastic stroma
Retains E-cadherin
May be associated with DCIS
Gland formation, necrosis, pleomorphism common

Invasive Lobular Carcinoma (ILC)

Second most common invasive type
Dyscohesive cells, single-file (Indian file) pattern
Loss of E-cadherin

Often bilateral and multifocal
